h1: The 6 Best Pressure Cookers Under $150 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Pressure Cooker Under $150: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six pressure cookers under $150, from 6-quart Instant Pots to compact 3-quart and stovetop models for small kitchens.
summary: The Instant Pot Duo Plus 6-quart is the best pressure cooker under $150 for most households: nine functions and a stainless steel pot. The Cosori matches its size and function count for less, and the Instant Pot Pro is the only one with sous vide. The Duo Mini suits small kitchens, and the Hawkins is a no-electronics stovetop cooker.
intro: A $150 ceiling sounds generous until you notice that most of the useful pressure cookers cost well below it. Spending the full amount rarely buys better pressure cooking. It buys extra presets, an app, or a mode like sous vide that many owners try twice and forget. What actually decides the purchase is size and format, and price comes a distant third.

We reviewed six cookers on paper, covering electric multi-cookers from Instant Pot and Cosori plus a stovetop design. Rankings reflect capacity, inner pot material, listed functions and how well each suits a particular kind of cook, based on the spec sheet and owner reports. Pot material and safety features counted because they decide how long a cooker stays pleasant to use.

products.name: Instant Pot Duo Plus 6-Qt 9-in-1 Electric Pressure Cooker, Stainless Steel
products.verdict: The six-quart workhorse that covers nearly every weeknight job.
products.description:
The Instant Pot Duo Plus is a six-quart, nine-in-one electric pressure cooker with a stainless steel inner pot and more presets than the base Duo. Six quarts feeds a family of three to five, and stainless steel tolerates metal utensils and scraping, which coated pots do not. Extra presets mean fewer manual adjustments on rice and beans.

It ranks first because it combines the right size with a durable pot at a mid-range price. The Cosori costs less with a ceramic pot, and the Pro costs more for sous vide.

Buy it for a household of three to five that wants one dependable cooker. The caveat is that there is no sous vide mode and some presets go unused. Skip it if you cook for one or two and want a smaller footprint.
products.idealFor: Households of three to five who want one dependable cooker.
products.skipIf: You cook for one or two people and want a smaller footprint.

products.name: Cosori Pressure Cooker 6QT, 9-in-1, Ceramic Coating Pot, 12 Safety Features
products.verdict: Matches the big names on size and functions, then leaves budget in your pocket.
products.description:
The Cosori is a six-quart, nine-in-one cooker with a ceramic-coated inner pot and twelve listed safety features. Matching the Duo Plus on size and function count while charging less leaves budget for a spare gasket and accessories. A coated pot is easy to clean, but it asks for gentler tools.

It ranks second because the brand is less familiar than Instant Pot and the coating can wear if you use metal utensils. The Duo Plus has a stainless pot that shrugs that off.

Buy it for a budget-minded family that wants six quarts without paying for extras. Skip it if you want a bare stainless pot that tolerates metal tools. Use wooden or silicone utensils and wash gently to protect the coating.
products.idealFor: Budget-minded families who want 6 quarts without paying for extras.
products.skipIf: You want a bare stainless pot that tolerates metal tools.

products.name: Instant Pot Pro 10-in-1 Pressure Cooker, Slow Cooker, Rice/Grain Cooker, Steamer, Sauté, Sous Vide, Yogurt Maker, Sterilizer, and Warmer, Includes App With Over 800 Recipes, Black, 6 Quart
products.verdict: The only pick here with sous vide, and priced like it.
products.description:
The Instant Pot Pro is a six-quart, ten-in-one cooker that adds sous vide to pressure cooking, slow cooking, rice, steaming, sauté, yogurt and warming, plus an app with over 800 recipes. Sous vide holds water at a steady temperature for a long cook, which suits steaks and eggs.

It ranks third because it costs more than its rivals and sous vide suits few cooks. It is the only pick here with that mode, and nothing else in the guide replicates it.

Buy it if you want sous vide and pressure cooking in one pot. Skip it if you only need pressure cooking and rice. For most kitchens, the Duo Plus does the daily jobs at lower cost.
products.idealFor: Cooks who want sous vide and pressure cooking in one pot.
products.skipIf: You only need pressure cooking and rice.

products.name: Instant Pot Duo 7-in-1 Electric Pressure Cooker, Slow Cooker, Rice, Steamer, Sauté, Yogurt Maker, Warmer & Sterilizer, Includes App With Over 800 Recipes, Stainless Steel, 6 Quart
products.verdict: The familiar full-size Duo, solid but outflanked by newer siblings.
products.description:
The Instant Pot Duo seven-in-one is a six-quart stainless steel cooker with pressure cook, slow cook, rice, steam, sauté, yogurt and warm functions, and an app with over 800 recipes. It is the original Duo layout at full size, with a format many people already know.

It ranks fourth because it has fewer presets than the Duo Plus and sits in a higher price bucket in this listing. Newer siblings do more for similar money.

Buy it if you want the familiar layout at full size. Skip it if you want more presets or a lower price. It does the core jobs well, but the Duo Plus makes better use of the same six quarts.
products.idealFor: Buyers who want the original Duo layout at full size.
products.skipIf: You want more presets or a lower price.

products.name: Instant Pot Duo 7-in-1 Mini Electric Pressure Cooker, Slow Rice Cooker, Steamer, Sauté, Yogurt Maker, Warmer & Sterilizer, Includes Free App with over 1900 Recipes, Stainless Steel, 3 Quart
products.verdict: A small-kitchen cooker with the biggest recipe library of the group.
products.description:
The Instant Pot Duo Mini is a three-quart, seven-in-one stainless steel cooker with an app that carries over 1,900 recipes, the largest library in the group. A three-quart pot suits one to three people and fits a small cabinet or counter.

It ranks fifth because three quarts is too small for families or batch cooking. Roasts and big batches of beans will not fit.

Buy it for a small kitchen cooking for one to three. Skip it if you regularly cook for four or more. Remember the two-thirds rule: three quarts of capacity means about two quarts of food.
products.idealFor: One to three people cooking in a small kitchen.
products.skipIf: You regularly cook for four or more.

products.name: Hawkins 3 Litre Contura Black Pressure Cooker, Hard Anodised Inner Lid Cooker, Handi Cooker, Black (CB30)
products.verdict: A no-electronics stovetop cooker for people who want fewer parts to fail.
products.description:
The Hawkins Contura is a three-liter stovetop pressure cooker with hard-anodized construction and an inner lid, with no electronics. Stovetop cookers heat quickly and have fewer parts to fail, which appeals to experienced cooks who like to manage the flame.

It ranks last because heat control is manual and there are no presets. It costs the least, but needs attention.

Buy it if you are an experienced stovetop cook who prefers simple gear. Skip it if you want set-and-forget cooking. The listing does not mention induction, so check compatibility before using it on an induction cooktop.
products.idealFor: Experienced stovetop cooks who prefer simple gear.

methodology.title: Capacity versus household
methodology.description: We matched quart size to how many people each cooker realistically feeds, since 3 and 6 quarts serve very different kitchens.

methodology.title: Inner pot material
methodology.description: Stainless steel, ceramic coating and hard-anodized aluminum wear differently, so we weighed long-term durability on paper.

methodology.title: Functions that matter
methodology.description: We counted modes but discounted ones few owners use, rewarding presets and features with a clear purpose.

methodology.title: Safety features listed
methodology.description: We checked what each listing says about lid locking and pressure release rather than assuming every cooker is equal.

methodology.title: Budget fit
methodology.description: We placed each model in its price bucket and asked whether the extra cost buys something concrete.

whatMatters.detail: Capacity is the usable volume of the pot, listed in quarts or liters. Cookers should never be filled past about two-thirds, so a 6-quart model gives roughly 4 quarts of food. Look for the number in the product title, then compare it against how many servings you cook at once, and leave room for foods that expand or foam.

Electric cookers regulate pressure and timing for you, while stovetop models rely on your burner and attention. Electric suits busy cooks who want to walk away, and stovetop heats faster and has fewer parts. The listing title usually says electric or stovetop, and induction compatibility is called out separately, if at all.

The inner pot touches your food and takes the abuse. Stainless steel tolerates metal utensils, ceramic coatings are easier to clean but can chip, and hard-anodized aluminum resists scratches. Check the specs list for the material name rather than relying on a marketing word like durable. The Cosori is ceramic coated, while the Duo models are stainless.

Numbers like 7-in-1 or 10-in-1 count modes such as slow cook, rice, yogurt and sous vide. More modes cost more, but pressure cooking, rice and sauté do most of the real work. Scan the title for the specific functions you want, since sous vide is only on the Pro here, and ignore the headline number.

Safety features include lid locks, pressure limiters and overheat protection, which keep the pot from releasing pressure unsafely. They matter most for beginners. Look for a listed safety count or a named certification on the page, such as the Cosori's twelve features, and be wary of listings that mention none.

faq.a: Six quarts suits most households and handles batch cooking. The 3-quart Duo Mini fits one to three people but leaves little room for whole roasts or large batches, so choose by the size of your household.

faq.q: Can I use the Hawkins on an induction cooktop?
faq.a: The listing for the Hawkins does not mention induction, so check compatibility before buying. Do not assume a stovetop cooker works on every cooktop, because induction needs a magnetic base and a flat bottom, and the listing says nothing either way.

faq.q: Is the Instant Pot Pro worth it over the Duo Plus?
faq.a: Only if you will use sous vide. Both are 6-quart electric cookers, but the Pro is in a higher price bucket for that extra mode. Otherwise the Duo Plus does more of the daily cooking for less, and you save the difference.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake with a new pressure cooker?
faq.a: Overfilling the pot. Most pots should stay under two-thirds full, and less for foods that foam such as beans or grains. A 6-quart Duo Plus gives roughly four quarts of usable food, so plan your batches accordingly.

faq.q: How do I care for a ceramic-coated pot?
faq.a: Use wooden or silicone utensils and wash gently. Avoid metal scrapers, which can wear down the coating on the Cosori. Check the manual for dishwasher guidance before putting the pot in, since heat can dull a coating.

They include lid locks and pressure controls, and the Cosori lists twelve safety features. Always follow the manual and release pressure as directed, and keep the vent clear of food and steam-sensitive items.

finalTake: The Instant Pot Duo Plus 6-quart is the right pressure cooker under $150 for most households, because it gets size, durability and presets right. The Cosori is the cheaper match, and the Pro is for sous vide fans. Choose capacity first, then the format.
